response.sql: WITH g AS (SELECT c.gender, COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS n FROM Invoices i JOIN Orders o ON o.order_id = i.order_id JOIN Customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id GROUP BY c.gender), a AS (SELECT AVG(n * 1.0) AS avg_n FROM g) SELECT AVG(g.n * 1.0) AS average_invoiced_orders, AVG(g.n - a.avg_n) AS average_excess_over_overall_average FROM g CROSS JOIN a WHERE g.n > a.avg_n

assumptions.assumption: An invoiced order is an order with at least one invoice, so it is counted once per order (COUNT DISTINCT order_id) even if it has several invoices.
A NULL gender forms its own group (GROUP BY keeps NULL as a group). An empty-string gender, if any exists, would be a separate group.

Genders above the average are those with a count strictly greater than the plain average of the per-gender counts. The single output row is the average count of those genders and the average of (count minus overall average) for them.

alternatives.interpretation: Count invoices per gender instead of distinct orders, so an order with several invoices counts several times.
alternatives.sql: WITH g AS (SELECT c.gender, COUNT(i.invoice_number) AS n FROM Invoices i JOIN Orders o ON o.order_id = i.order_id JOIN Customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id GROUP BY c.gender), a AS (SELECT AVG(n * 1.0) AS avg_n FROM g) SELECT AVG(g.n * 1.0) AS average_invoiced_orders, AVG(g.n - a.avg_n) AS average_excess_over_overall_average FROM g CROSS JOIN a WHERE g.n > a.avg_n
